intro: Taketa maps one stop for now: Noike, a spring-fed park in Kuju on the Kuju plateau, opened in 1873 as one of the first public parks in Japan and named a national scenic site in 2025. Two giant cedars flank the torii at its entrance, and Japan's forest tree breeding centre lists the shrine's cedar at about 800 years old and 41 metres tall. The pond beside them is fed by two volcanic springs that stay at 12 to 13 degrees all year.
meta_description: The cedars of Noike Shrine in Kuju, Taketa: a giant cedar about 800 years old and 41 m tall at the torii of a spring-fed park opened in 1873.
question_meta: Taketa's mapped tree is the cedar of Noike Shrine in Kuju, listed at about 800 years old, 41 metres tall and 7.2 metres round.
question_answer: The tree mapped at Taketa is the cedar of Noike Shrine, in Noike Park in Kuju. Japan's forest tree breeding centre lists it at an estimated 800 years old, 41 metres tall and 7.2 metres round. Two giant cedars flank the torii at the park entrance.
question_context: Noike was a shrine to a water deity long before it became a park. It opened as a public park in 1873, under the government decree that created Japan's first parks, and in March 2025 the national government designated it a scenic site. The park is small, about 250 metres from end to end, and a third of it is a pond fed by two springs from the volcanic Kuju plateau, which keep the water at 12 to 13 degrees in every season. Old cedars, tabu trees and Japanese andromeda grow along its banks. At the entrance a torii stands between two giant cedars. Japan's forest tree breeding centre lists the shrine's cedar at an estimated 800 years, 41 metres tall and 7.2 metres round; no second source gives an age, so the figure stays an estimate. The same centre runs a gene bank for giant trees, growing young trees from cuttings or grafts at an owner's request, and in March 2008 it returned young cedars grown from this one to the shrine. The park is free, and the drive from Bungo-Taketa Station takes about 25 minutes.

faq.q: Where are the cedars of Noike Shrine?
faq.a: At the entrance to Noike Park in Kuju, Taketa, Oita Prefecture, where a torii stands between two giant cedars.
Japan's forest tree breeding centre gives an estimated 800 years for the shrine's cedar. No second source gives an age, so treat it as an estimate.
By car: about 25 minutes from Bungo-Taketa Station on the JR Hohi Line.

trees.story:
Noike was a shrine to a water deity before it was anything else. In 1873 it became a public park under the government decree that created Japan's first parks, one of the earliest in the country, and in 2025 the national government named it a scenic site. Two springs from the volcanic Kuju plateau feed its pond, and they run at 12 to 13 degrees in every season.

The torii at the park entrance stands between two giant cedars. Japan's forest tree breeding centre lists the shrine's cedar at an estimated 800 years, 41 metres tall and 7.2 metres round, which no second source confirms, so take the age as an estimate. The same centre runs a gene bank for giant trees: at an owner's request it grows young trees from cuttings or grafts, keeps some and gives some back. In March 2008 it returned young cedars grown from this one to the shrine.

The park is small, about 250 metres from end to end, and a third of it is water. Stand at the torii and look up: the cedar's crown spreads far above the bamboo grove beside it. Old cedars, tabu trees and Japanese andromeda line the pond behind.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as one of the two giant cedars that flank the torii at the entrance to Noike Park, with a bamboo grove beside it.
